name: Mind-reading machine
definition: A machine that reads a person's specific thoughts, memories or images directly from their brain.

milestones2.what: ATR labs in Kyoto reconstructed 10x10-pixel images a person viewed from brain signals.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: allowed researchers to reconstruct images from brain signals at a resolution of 10×10 pixels

milestones2.note: Only seen images are decoded, not specific thoughts or memories, so it is a partial fit; Nishimoto 2011 movie reconstruction is later. Yang Dan 1999 decoded images from cat thalamus (animal, rejected).
milestones2.check_note: Earlier decoding of seen orientations (Kamitani and Tong 2005) decodes simple features, not images; Yang Dan 1999 cat thalamus is animal. Partial fit (seen images, not thoughts), but nothing earlier fits better.

doubt: 2008 ATR reconstruction of 10x10-pixel images a person sees is a stretch: it reconstructs what was seen, not specific thoughts or memories. Carries #8, #12, #15.
search_hints: Test case for fit: reconstructing what a person sees is not reading memories or thoughts. Search for decoding of imagined content, memories or specific thoughts.

name: Central computer directing many robots
definition: A single computer or master robot that coordinates and directs a whole population of robots.

milestones2.what: Walgreens installed a Kiva mobile-robot fulfilment system at Mount Vernon, Illinois

sources.title: Amazon Robotics
sources.quote: Walgreens installed one at its distribution center in Mount Vernon, Illinois, in 2007

milestones2.note: Too late probably: AGV fleets under central computer traffic control existed in the 1970s (Volvo Kalmar 1972-74 seen only in search summaries, central control not confirmed). Staples 2006 not confirmed.
milestones2.check_note: Possibly too late: wire-guided AGV fleets (Volvo Kalmar 1972-74, Tetra Pak Lund 1976 with 20 AGVs and a control system per Wikipedia NDC) existed earlier, but no fetchable source states a central computer directing them, so not substituted. Staples 2006 not confirmed.

doubt: 2007 Walgreens/Kiva is one year later than the first pass's 2006 Staples/Kiva and carries four of the top 20. Centrally dispatched AGV fleets in factories and warehouses date from the 1970s-80s, but the checker found no fetchable source.
search_hints: Centrally dispatched AGV (automated guided vehicle) fleets in 1970s-80s factories and warehouses, directed by a central computer (e.g. FMS lines, Volvo Kalmar 1974, computer-controlled AGV systems in Computerworld / sim_ industrial-engineering periodicals); anything earlier than Kiva (2006-07).

name: Automatic dictation transcription
definition: A machine that listens to dictation and produces the written or typed text automatically.

milestones2.what: Kyoto University's Sonotype phonetic typewriter, which prints out spoken words, reached the prototype stage (reported in Electronics, 1960-61; handled 100 Japanese monosyllables in its early version).

sources.title: Phonetic Typewriter Nears Practical Use
sources.quote: Development of a phonetic typewriter—one which will print out spoken words—has progressed at Kyoto University, Japan

milestones2.note: Tangora (mid-1980s) is far too late. Earlier fit: Kyoto Sonotype phonetic typewriter, prototype by 1960-61 (article cites an Electronics report of 27 May 1960). Even earlier is probably Olson and Belar's RCA phonetic typewriter (J. Acoust. Soc. Am., Nov 1956, single talker, ~10 syllables) but I could not fetch a page to quote it, so 1961 is the earliest sourced; true date likely 1956.

milestones2.what: Dragon Dictate released as a consumer dictation product (discrete words, DOS).

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1990 – Dragon Dictate, a consumer product released in 1990.

milestones2.note: First pass said 1997 NaturallySpeaking, which was the first continuous-speech product, not the first dictation product. The same Wikipedia list gives 1987 'a recognizer from Kurzweil Applied Intelligence' (Kurzweil's medical-report dictation system); the line has no detail, so I could not confirm it as dictation and kept 1990. An earlier 1987 or 1984-85 product may fit. No mass_adoption sourced: dictation by speech only became routine on smartphones in the 2010s, but no fetched source states it.
milestones2.check_note: Kurzweil 1987 recognizer (same Wikipedia list) has no detail to confirm it was dictation; Dragon Dictate 1990 kept. Looked for an earlier product and found no fetchable source. Prior: First pass said 1997 NaturallySpeaking, which was the first continuous-speech product, not the first dictation product. The same Wikipedia list gives 1987 'a recognizer from Kurzweil Applied Intelligence' (Kurzweil's medical-report dictation system); the line has no detail, so I could not confirm it as dictation and kept 1990. An earlier 1987 or 1984-85 product may fit. No mass_adoption sourced: dictation by speech only became routine on smartphones in the 2010s, but no fetched source states it.

doubt: Date the agents called approximate: 1961 (RCA's 1956 phonetic typewriter is probably earlier, but unsourced).
search_hints: RCA's 1956 phonetic typewriter (Olson and Belar) and other 1950s-60s typing-from-speech machines; first dictation product in use.

name: Retina and iris recognition
definition: A machine that identifies a person by scanning the patterns of the eye.

milestones2.what: EyeDentify's retinal scanner went on the market as a commercial model in 1981 (specific scanner means patented 1978), after the device concept emerged in 1975.

sources.title: Retinal scan
sources.quote: In 1978, specific means for a retinal scanner was patented, followed by a commercial model in 1981.

milestones2.note: The concept covers retina as well as iris; retina scanning predates Daugman's 1994 iris algorithms. 1981 is the first dated working (commercial) retinal scanner found; Flom and Safir's iris concept and the 1935 Simon-Goldstein retina idea had no working device. A demonstration may precede 1981 (patent 1978) but no dated demonstration found.

name: Computerized information retrieval
definition: A machine that stores very large collections of records or documents and finds the items matching a query in seconds.

milestones2.what: Lockheed completed the earliest form of Dialog under Roger K. Summit, an online interactive retrieval system

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

milestones2.note: Earlier candidate: MEDLARS (NLM, 1964), a batch computer retrieval service, not interactive 'in seconds'; also pre-computer mechanical retrieval (Goldberg's Statistical Machine, 1931) rejected as not computerized.

milestones2.what: Lockheed's interactive Dialog system (Roger Summit) was tested on NASA's STAR database at Ames in 1966, cutting searches from 14 hours to a few minutes; this became NASA RECON.

sources.title: Roger K. Summit
sources.quote: Information searches within the NASA STAR database went from taking 14 hours, plus shipping and handling, to a few minutes with Summit's Dialog system.

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

milestones2.note: Replaces MEDLINE late 1971: Dialog was online and interactive on a large NASA database in 1966 (Ames experiment, NASA contract 1966). Result time is 'a few minutes' not strictly seconds, and 1966 was an experiment before RECON (1967 award); MEDLARS 1964 was batch. Original note: Rejected earlier: MEDLARS 1964 (launched by NLM, 'first large-scale, computer-based, retrospective search service available to the general public') was a real service but batch-mode, so it does not meet 'in seconds'. Dialog commercial service started ~1972 (not sourced). If batch counts, practical use is 1964.

name: Robot police and security guards
definition: Robots that patrol, guard buildings, check credentials or arrest people on behalf of authorities.

milestones2.what: Knightscope shipped its first autonomous security patrol robot

sources.title: Knightscope
sources.quote: Knightscope shipped their first robot in 2015.

milestones2.note: Almost certainly too late. Earlier: Denning Sentry (mid-1980s), ROBART I (c. 1982), PROWLER armed sentry (developed from 1983); I could not fetch usable dated sources for them.
milestones2.check_note: Knightscope 2015 is probably late. Earlier: Denning Sentry, introduced 1985 per Computer History Museum ('designed this robot as a security guard patrolling for up to 14 hours'), but CHM says the product did not succeed and press said none were sold, so practical use is not shown; Cybermotion SR2 at LACMA, ROBART and PROWLER could not be dated or sourced. A human should look for first deployed Cybermotion/Denning units.

doubt: 2015 Knightscope: the checker named likely earlier security robots (1980s) but could not source them.
search_hints: 1980s security robots (Denning Mobile Robotics sentry 1985-87, RoboGuard, Prowler, others) and when one was first actually used on patrol by a customer.

name: Question-answering computer
definition: A computer holding broad knowledge that answers arbitrary factual questions put to it in ordinary language.

milestones2.what: MIT's START natural-language system went online on the Internet in 1993 and answered English questions on many topics (Boris Katz, MIT)

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: Boris Katz is the creator of the START information processing system (since 1993 - on the Internet)

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: START natural language system that allows the user to access various types of information using English

milestones2.note: START (1993) answered open-ended English questions about places, people, movies and more over the Web, an earlier broad-domain system than Watson 2011; its knowledge came from hand-annotated sources so breadth is limited (hence low). BASEBALL 1961, LUNAR 1971, SHRDLU, Unix Consultant and LILOG are narrow-domain; Ask Jeeves 1996 matched questions to web pages; Wolfram Alpha 2009 and Watson 2011 are later.

name: Touchscreen and gesture interface
definition: Controlling a machine by touching a screen or panel, or by hand gestures and gloves read by sensors.

milestones2.what: E. A. Johnson (Royal Radar Establishment, Malvern) published a finger-driven capacitive touchscreen for air traffic control

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: He described his work on capacitive touchscreens in a short article published in 1965

milestones2.note: Earlier: AT&T Harmon 1962 patent for a light-beam stylus touchscreen (patent only, not shown working). Data gloves: Sayre Glove 1977, later. Light pens (1950s) are pointing devices, not touch.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier: Philco 1946 stylus patent (overlay on TV, not touch input), AT&T Harmon 1962 light-beam patent (patent only, no working system shown), Graham 1963 light-pen patent. Johnson 1965 is the first finger-driven touchscreen per Wikipedia. Gesture side: nothing earlier controlling a machine fits (theremin is a musical instrument, not machine control).

milestones2.what: PLATO IV terminals, introduced at the University of Illinois in 1972, had a built-in 16x16 infrared touch panel students used to answer questions

sources.title: PLATO (computer system)
sources.quote: In 1972, with the introduction of PLATO IV, Bitzer declared general success

sources.title: PLATO (computer system)
sources.quote: Touch panel: A 16×16 grid infrared touch panel, allowing students to answer questions by touching anywhere on the screen.

milestones2.note: CERN's touchscreen was put to use in 1973; PLATO IV touch panels were part of the 1972 classroom system (Wikipedia Touchscreen dates the optical patent filing to 1972). Johnson's ATC touchscreen and the 1970 Telefunken device were described in the 1960s-70 but no fetched source gives deployed use earlier.

milestones2.what: Touchscreen phones were rapidly gaining popularity by 2009 after the 2007 LG Prada and iPhone

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: By 2009, touchscreen-enabled phones were rapidly gaining popularity

milestones2.note: Date is a judgement (2007-2010). iPhone announced Jan 2007; first-pass 2007 date replaced by when popularity is stated.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier touchscreens in ATMs, kiosks, HP-150 (1983), IBM Simon (1993), Nintendo DS (2004) were niche or early-stage, not routine use by ordinary people; 2009 majority of smartphones shipping with touchscreens (Wikipedia) supports 2007-2009 as the mass-adoption window.

name: Robot vacuum cleaner and lawn mower
definition: A small autonomous machine that cleans floors or mows a lawn on its own.

milestones2.what: Whirlpool demonstrated a track-following robotic floor sweeper concept (Donald Moore's 1957 patent) at the American National Exhibition in Moscow

sources.title: Robotic vacuum cleaner
sources.quote: Whirlpool demonstrated the concept at the 1959 American National Exhibition but did not bring it to market.

milestones2.note: Follows a track under the floor, so only a loose fit to 'on its own'. Later: MowBot 1969, Electrolux Trilobite 1996, Roomba 2002. Heinlein 1956 was fiction.

milestones2.what: MowBot, autonomous robotic lawn mower patented by S. Lawrence Bellinger, sold for about $800

sources.title: Robotic lawn mower
sources.quote: In 1969, the MowBot was introduced and patented by S Lawrence Bellinger having many features of today's most popular products.

milestones2.note: No earlier robot mower or vacuum on sale found in the pages read. Trilobite (1996) and Roomba (2002) are later. Whether MowBot was truly autonomous rests on this one source.

name: Neural implant and cyborg augmentation
definition: An electronic device implanted in or joined to the human body or brain to restore or extend senses, memory or ability.

milestones2.what: Djourno and Eyries in France invented the original cochlear implant, stimulating the auditory nerve electrically.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: André Djourno and Charles Eyriès invented the original cochlear implant in 1957.

milestones2.note: Earlier than the first-pass House 1961. Cardiac pacemaker implants (1958) are body implants not neural/sensory, so rejected for this concept.

milestones2.what: Hochmair's multichannel cochlear implant was first implanted in a person in Vienna, followed by Clark's in 1978; both were commercialized.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: with the Hochmairs' device first implanted in a person in December 1977 and Clark's in August 1978

milestones2.note: House/3M single-channel devices were marketed from 1972 and FDA-approved for adults in 1984 (not verified with a fetched quote), which may be earlier practical use. Date here is a weak proxy.

name: Service robot for the public
definition: A robot that serves customers or the public as a waiter, bartender, clerk, receptionist or guide.
doubt: No milestone survived verification. Hospital delivery robots (late 1980s) and others exist, but no page could be fetched; 63 pairs score 0. A gap in sourcing, not in history.
search_hints: 1980s hospital delivery robots (Transitions Research Corp. HelpMate, first hospital use), other robots serving the public (restaurants, hotels, museums) before 2014.
